title: Follow an edge
objective: Follow the changing contour of a shoe by drawing the edges you observe rather than a remembered outline.

warmup.instructions: Place one shoe so its toe, heel, collar, and sole are visible. Spend 2 minutes drawing one connected edge from heel toward the collar, looking back at the shoe before each new section. Spend 2 minutes following the sole near the toe. Take 2 minutes to compare those edges with the shoe; mark each clearest change of direction. Use the final minute to note which turn you will check in the main drawing. Total: 7 minutes.

explanation: A contour is the visible boundary where the shoe meets its background. Follow it as a sequence of edges that turn, flatten, or curve; do not complete a shoe outline from memory.

Pause when the direction changes and look back at the shoe. Draw the outside edge first, compare one turn, then restate the contour in a fresh space. Add only a few interior edges that help identify this shoe.

exercise.instructions:
1. Set one shoe at a steady viewpoint. Choose a page direction that gives it room and keep the shoe still. (3 min)
2. Study the toe, heel, opening, and sole. Make a light, recognizable drawing by following the outer contour in connected sections. Pause at a change of direction and look back at the shoe before continuing. (12 min)
3. Compare the outline with the shoe. Circle one mismatch at a clear turn, such as the toe angle, heel curve, or slope of the sole. (4 min)
4. In a fresh space, draw the shoe again from the same view. Follow the contour slowly and focus on the turn you chose to correct. Keep the first drawing visible. (12 min)
5. Add only a few interior edges that help identify the shoe, such as its opening or one seam. Compare the outline once more and stop before adding small details. (4 min)

reflection: Which contour turn most changed the shoe's overall shape?
In the second drawing, which edge came closer to what you observed?
extension: Repeat the contour study from another side of the same shoe, watching for one edge that changes direction in a new way.

teaching.whyItMatters: A shoe has a contour with turns, flats, and curves. Tracking those changes makes the drawing specific to the shoe in front of you.
teaching.connections: Lesson 1 taught you to keep and compare an initial attempt. Here, slow that comparison down to a few observed edges; Lesson 3 will use the same attention to shapes around a subject.

deepDive: Treat the contour as a route your eye follows, not as a symbol you finish in one remembered gesture. A shoe is familiar, so the mind may supply a generic toe, heel, or opening before you have checked this particular one. Instead, look for where one edge direction changes into another. A long curve can flatten near the sole; a collar can turn more sharply than the heel; a toe may rise or angle down. These changes are useful landmarks because a small shift at a turn can alter the whole shoe silhouette. Keep the view fixed while you compare the drawing and the object, so you can tell whether the mismatch is in the line you chose or in the viewpoint.

The outside contour and the shoe's interior seams do different jobs. The contour tells you how the shoe sits against its background; seams, laces, and openings help identify its parts. If you add all those details at once, the page fills before the large shape is clear. First make a connected outline in manageable sections and pause at a visible turn. After the first pass, pick one turn you can compare directly with the real shoe, then restate the outline in another space. Only after that check should you add a few interior edges. This order gives your eye a chance to notice shape before detail and leaves the first drawing available for comparison. This makes the review manageable and leaves room for more independent choices later.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing a tidy shoe outline from memory before checking its turns.
commonMistakes.lookFor: The toe, heel, collar, and sole all look smoothly rounded and generic. Return to the shoe and mark where the direction actually changes.

selfCheck: Can you point to the clearest direction change in the shoe and in your drawing?
Did you keep the same viewpoint while comparing the first and second outlines?
Do a few interior edges identify the shoe without obscuring its outer contour?
